This,
The main methods for grinding output from meshes are in the “read this first” tutorial on r-inla.org, using inla.mesh.project and inla.mesh.projector, and optional also inla.mesh.lattice to define the lattice that you want the output for.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] re: Code for SPDE species distribution model
parts:
I wrote a function to do that in my PointedSDMs package:
<https://github.com/oharar/PointedSDMs/blob/master/R/MakeProjectionGrid.R>
(based on the code Finn pointed to). Essentially, you add your grid
into the model, but with NAs in the response, and then you have to
extract the predictions from the INLA object, which you can do by
tagging everything.

This means the projections are done at the same time as the model
fitting - I should probably add a function (also based on the code
Finn pointed to) that does this after the model fitting.

Bob

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] re: Code for SPDE species distribution model
parts:
For large models, it’s better if the gridding can be done after the inla call instead of inside it, to keep the model size down.

If there are no high resolution covariates, one can let inla predict on the mesh nodes only, and then apply the grinding on the output. (With this method, one can grid the standard deviations to get spatially appropriate uncertainties, not provided by the other approaches that result in lower std.dev. in the middle of triangles.)

If there are high resolution covariates, the gridding is best done by sampling with inla.posterios.sample(), and then do gridding based on the samples.

The needed projection matrix is the same in all three approaches. The difference lies in where/when it is applied.

Finn
